full_judgment:
2 The plaintiff-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 filed the mortgage suit for recovery of mortgage money. Their case inter alia was that the plaintiff No. 3 Nawab Ali Ahmed was the owner in possession with other co-sharers of the suit land and he borrowed Rs. 1599/-from one Tarani Mohan Gope, predecessor of pro-defendant Nos. 5 and 6 and executed a deed of mortgage to Tarani on 8.8.192 1 corresponding to 23rd Sraban 1328 B.S. in respect of his share in the suit land, vide Ext. 2. The money was to be repaid by Kartik 1329 B S Tarani sold the mortgage to Nazitunnessa, wife of the mortgagor Nawab Ali Ahmed by a registered kabala, dated 2-6-1938, vide Ext. 1 and handed over the mortgage document to Islazituanessa Mortgagr Nawab Ali Ahmed has paid money on account of interest to Tarani and Nazitunnessa on various dates and he wrote the endorsement vide Ext. 3 series on the back of the mortgage deed Ext, 2 Nazitunessa died leaving her husband Nawab All Ahmed, plaintiff No. 2, and her son plaintiff No 1 as her only heir who became owners of the mortgage of the suit holding. The superior landlord Bridhi Chand Gouthi, auction purchased the suit holding in a rent sale, but no notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act was served upon the plaintiffs of Tarani or anybody else to annul the encumbrance. So the mortgage still subsists. Al-though the plaintiff No. 2 mortgaged the suit land possession remained with him all throughout. After rent purchase Bridhi Chand Gouthi gifted his rent-receiving interest to the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 who in turn granted pattern in respect of some portion of suit land to the defendant No. 3. The defendant Nos. 1 to 3 have never got possession of the suit land. Rs. 2480/- is still due on account of mortgage money. Hence the suit to recover this amount by selling the mortgaged property in auction if the decretal due be not paid. 

 13. Mr. A.A. Mannan learned Advocate for the respondent Nos. 1-2 does not dispute the principles enunciated in the aforesaid cases but he seeks to make a distinction by submitting that the case cited relate to circumstances where there has been a voluntary transfer of interest by the mortgagor. These decisions do not apply to involuntary transfer as in the present case. Of the three cases cited by Mr. Sarker, however, it appears that the Full Bench case of Madras Miah Court deals with involuntary transfer and the other two with voluntary transfers. It appears that the principles enunciated in the cases cited before me apply to every form of, transfer volunary or involuntary. Mr. M.A. Mannan is unable to cite any authority in support of his contention that acknowledgment made by a mortgagor after an involuntary transfer of his interest binds the transferee. Mr. Mannan in seeking to make a further distinction submits that the respondents have not accepted the fact that there has been a transfer of interest in the suit land. He has cited several cases to bring home the point that in a mortgage suit paramount title can't be determined. That is so with respect to third parties and but I find from the plaint that the plaintiff-respondents suit has proceeded on the assumption that there has been a rent sale of the suit land and that no notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act has been served to annul any encumbrances. Mr. Sarker, on the other hand, pointed out by reference to the written statement and to Ext's. Dl, CI and B2 that the mortgagor defendant No. 4 filed an application for setting aside the sale and lost it. That being the position, it appears to me that even the plaintiff-respondents have proceeded in this case on the assumption that there has been a rent sale and that the defendant Nos. 1-3 are the doneness of the auction purchasers. 

 14. Mr. Mannan has next contended that neither the mortgagor nor the mortgagee having received notice of the rent sale the mortgagee will follow the mortgagor and if the mortgagor fails to pay the mortgage money he will follow the mortgaged property. The mortgagee having had no notice of the rent sale, acknowledgments granted by the mortgagor after the rent sale are fully effective and binding upon the auction purchaser and his successors. I do not think the submissions, under the facts and circumstances of the case, are correct. The auction purchaser having not annulled the encumbrance under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act the mortgage still subsists but it is no longer the mortgagor who is liable to pay to the mortgagee. The auction-purchaser having not paid any principal or interest to the mortgagee or his assignee the endorsement given by the mortgagor will not bind auction purchaser. These endorsements were given after the rent-sale, after the mortgagor lost his interest in the suit land.
